question: Which agency appoints notaries public in New York?

options.text: The New York Department of State (Secretary of State)
options.why: Correct. Executive Law §130 gives the Secretary of State the power to appoint and commission notaries.

options.text: The county clerk
options.why: Wrong. The county clerk keeps the notary's signature and commission on file but doesn't appoint notaries.

options.text: The Appellate Division of the Supreme Court
options.why: Wrong. The Appellate Division admits attorneys; it doesn't commission notaries.

options.text: The Governor's office directly
options.why: Wrong. Appointment is delegated to the Secretary of State, not exercised by the Governor directly.

explanation: The Secretary of State, through the Department of State's Division of Licensing Services, appoints New York notaries.

refs.title: N.Y. Exec. Law §130 (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 5)

question: How long is a New York notary public commission?

options.text: Four years
options.why: Correct. A New York commission runs for four years.

options.text: Two years
options.why: Wrong. Too short; New York uses a four-year term.

options.text: Ten years
options.why: Wrong. Ten years is the record-retention period for electronic notarizations, not the term.

options.text: Until the notary turns 70
options.why: Wrong. Commissions have a fixed term, not an age limit.

explanation: A New York notary is commissioned for a term of four years.

refs.title: N.Y. Exec. Law §130 (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 5)

question: What is the minimum age for a New York notary public?

options.why: Correct. Applicants must be at least 18 years old.
Wrong. 21 isn't the requirement.
Wrong. Minors can't hold a notary commission.
Wrong. That's far above the minimum.

explanation: An applicant must be at least 18 years of age.
source: NY DOS Notary Public Application Guidance

question: A Connecticut resident works full time at an office in Manhattan. May they apply to be a New York notary?

options.text: Yes; a non-resident with an office or place of business in New York may apply
options.why: Correct. Residency or a New York office or place of business satisfies the requirement.

options.text: No; only New York residents may apply
options.why: Wrong. The law expressly allows non-residents with a New York office or place of business.

options.text: Only if they pass the Connecticut notary exam first
options.why: Wrong. Another state's exam has no bearing on a New York commission.

options.text: Only if they are an attorney
options.why: Wrong. Attorneys are exempt from the exam, but non-attorneys with a NY office can apply too.

explanation: Applicants must be New York residents or have an office or place of business in New York.

refs.title: N.Y. Exec. Law §130 (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 5)

question: Which applicant is exempt from taking the New York notary exam?

options.text: An attorney admitted to practice in New York
options.why: Correct. NY attorneys (and certain court clerks) don't need to take the exam.

options.text: A notary commissioned in another state
options.why: Wrong. Another state's commission doesn't exempt anyone from the New York exam.

options.text: A licensed real estate broker
options.why: Wrong. Real estate licensees still have to pass the exam.

options.text: Anyone with a college degree
options.why: Wrong. Education level doesn't create an exemption.

explanation: Attorneys admitted in New York and certain clerks of the Unified Court System are exempt from the notary exam.
source: N.Y. Exec. Law §130; NY DOS Notary Public FAQs

question: What score is needed to pass the New York notary public exam?

options.why: Correct. The Department of State requires 70% to pass.
Wrong. Below the passing score.
Wrong. Above the actual requirement.
Wrong. A perfect score isn't required.

explanation: Applicants must score at least 70% on the multiple-choice notary exam.

question: Must a New York notary obtain a surety bond?

options.text: No; New York does not require a notary bond
options.why: Correct. Unlike Texas, California and Florida, New York has no bond requirement.
Wrong. That's the Texas bond amount.
Wrong. That's the California bond amount.
Wrong. That's the Florida bond amount.

explanation: New York does not require notaries to be bonded, although a notary remains personally liable for misconduct.
source: N.Y. Exec. Law §§130–131; NY DOS Become a Notary Public

question: Where is a New York notary's commission and signature filed so it can be checked later?

options.text: With the county clerk of the county where the notary qualified
options.why: Correct. The commission and signature are filed with the county clerk, who can then certify the notary's official character.

options.text: With the Office of Court Administration
options.why: Wrong. Court administration doesn't keep notary files.

options.text: With the notary's employer
options.why: Wrong. Employers have no official record-keeping role.

options.text: With the New York State Bar Association
options.why: Wrong. The Bar is a private association of lawyers.

explanation: The commission and specimen signature are filed with the county clerk where the notary qualified, which allows the clerk to authenticate the notary's signature.

question: Where may a New York notary perform notarial acts?

options.text: Anywhere in New York State
options.why: Correct. Jurisdiction is statewide, not limited to the county of qualification.

options.text: Only in the county where they qualified
options.why: Wrong. The county of qualification matters for filing, not for where the notary can act.

options.text: Only in New York City
options.why: Wrong. The commission covers the whole state.

options.text: Anywhere in the United States
options.why: Wrong. A New York commission doesn't authorize acts in other states.

explanation: A New York notary may act anywhere within the State of New York.

question: A person was convicted of a felony and has not received a pardon, certificate of relief from disabilities or certificate of good conduct. May they be appointed?

options.text: No; the conviction disqualifies them unless relief is granted
options.why: Correct. Felony convictions (and certain listed offenses) disqualify an applicant unless they have obtained executive pardon or a certificate of relief or good conduct.

options.text: Yes, if five years have passed
options.why: Wrong. The passage of time alone doesn't remove the disqualification.

options.text: Yes, if they pass the exam with 90%
options.why: Wrong. Exam scores don't override eligibility rules.

options.text: Yes, if their employer vouches for them
options.why: Wrong. An employer's support doesn't cure a disqualifying conviction.

explanation: A felony conviction disqualifies an applicant unless they receive a pardon or a certificate of relief from disabilities or of good conduct.

question: Who may remove a New York notary from office for misconduct?

options.text: The Secretary of State, after notice and an opportunity to be heard
options.why: Correct. Executive Law §130 lets the Secretary of State suspend or remove a notary for misconduct.

options.text: The notary's employer
options.why: Wrong. An employer can stop a notary from acting for the business but can't remove a commission.

options.text: The county clerk
options.why: Wrong. Clerks keep records but have no removal power.

options.text: Any judge, without a hearing
options.why: Wrong. Removal is an administrative action by the Secretary of State with due process.

explanation: The Secretary of State may suspend or remove a notary for misconduct after the notary has had a chance to be heard.

refs.title: N.Y. Exec. Law §130 (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 6)

question: A non-resident notary qualified on the strength of a New York office. They close the office and no longer work in New York. What happens to the commission?

options.text: The office is vacated; they are no longer eligible to hold the commission
options.why: Correct. A non-resident's eligibility depends on keeping a New York office or place of business; without it the commission is vacated.

options.text: Nothing; the commission runs until it expires
options.why: Wrong. Eligibility must continue throughout the term.

options.text: They may keep notarizing for New York documents only
options.why: Wrong. Losing eligibility ends authority for every document.

options.text: The commission automatically becomes a Connecticut commission
options.why: Wrong. No state transfers commissions automatically.

explanation: A non-resident who stops having a New York office or place of business no longer meets the eligibility requirement, and the office is vacated.

refs.title: N.Y. Exec. Law §130 (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 5)

question: A New York notary changes their name after marriage. What should they do?

options.text: Notify the Department of State of the change so the commission record is updated
options.why: Correct. The Department of State must be told so the official record matches the name the notary signs.

options.text: Nothing; keep signing with the old name forever
options.why: Wrong. The commission record has to reflect the change.

options.text: Resign and take the exam again
options.why: Wrong. A name change doesn't require retaking the exam.

options.text: Ask the county clerk to issue a new commission
options.why: Wrong. The county clerk doesn't issue commissions.

explanation: Changes of name or address are reported to the Department of State, which updates the commission record.

question: Is a New York notary allowed to notarize a document that will be used in another state?

options.text: Yes, as long as the notarial act is performed in New York
options.why: Correct. Authority depends on where the act happens, not where the document will be used.

options.text: No, only documents used in New York
options.why: Wrong. Documents for use elsewhere are routinely notarized in New York.

options.text: Only with the other state's permission
options.why: Wrong. No permission from another state is needed.

options.text: Only if the document is in English and Spanish
options.why: Wrong. Language has nothing to do with where a document may be used.

explanation: A New York notary may notarize documents for use anywhere, provided the act takes place in New York.

refs.title: N.Y. Exec. Law §135 (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 7)

question: A notary's commission expired, but they didn't realize it and kept notarizing for two weeks. A person relied on one of those notarizations in good faith. Under Executive Law §142-a, what is the effect?

options.text: The act is not invalid solely because the commission had expired, for those relying on it in good faith
options.why: Correct. §142-a protects people who rely in good faith on acts affected by certain defects, including an expired term. The notary may still face discipline.

options.text: The act is void and the document must be re-signed
options.why: Wrong. §142-a exists precisely to protect good-faith reliance on such acts.

options.text: The act is valid and the notary did nothing wrong
options.why: Wrong. Protecting the public's reliance doesn't excuse the notary's acting without authority.

options.text: The act becomes valid only if the notary pays a fine
options.why: Wrong. Validity under §142-a doesn't depend on any payment.

explanation: Executive Law §142-a keeps acts from being invalid because of certain defects, such as an expired term, for people relying on them in good faith. The notary must still not act without a valid commission.

refs.title: N.Y. Exec. Law §142-a (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 10)

question: What must a New York notary do before acting under a new commission?

options.text: Take the oath of office, which is part of the application
options.why: Correct. Applicants take the constitutional oath of office as part of the commissioning process.

options.text: Buy an embossing seal
options.why: Wrong. New York doesn't require an embossing seal.

options.text: Purchase a $10,000 bond
options.why: Wrong. New York has no bond requirement.

options.text: Register with the town board
options.why: Wrong. Town boards play no part in notary commissions.

explanation: Every applicant takes an oath of office; there is no bond and no seal requirement in New York.
source: N.Y. Exec. Law §131; N.Y. Pub. Off. Law §15
